title: Product Manager - AI

hero.h1: AI product manager interviews: what the job asks for
hero.p: You do not need to train models, but you must reason about them. This track covers the AI concepts a product manager is probed on, how to frame, spec, evaluate and launch AI features, and a 6-week plan of 3 hours on weekdays and 5 on weekends.

jd.lead: This is a synthesis of requirements that recur in AI product manager postings, not a statistical count. Check it against the three or four postings you are actually targeting and adjust the weights.

rows.name: AI product sense: when AI is the right solution, and which kind (rules, classic ML, LLM)
rows.where: Case questions: "would you build this with AI?" and use-case prioritisation

rows.name: LLM working knowledge: tokens, context, prompting, RAG, agents, tool use
rows.where: Technical rounds with engineers; you must be credible, not hands-on deep

rows.name: Evaluation: golden sets, quality metrics, error analysis, online experiments
rows.where: "How do you know it works?" is the standard AI PM question

rows.name: Writing specs for non-deterministic features: PRDs with eval criteria and failure handling
AI UX and trust: uncertainty, citations, fallbacks, feedback loops, latency
Economics: cost per request, latency, model choice, build vs buy, pricing
Safety, privacy, governance: prompt injection, PII, regulation, red teaming
rows.where: Working with legal, security and trust teams

rows.name: Strategy and leadership: moats, roadmaps under uncertainty, stakeholder communication
Fine-tuning, MCP, vector databases, model routing, distillation

jd.note: Written from general knowledge of the role, not from a fresh scrape of postings. Treat the tiers as a starting point.

conceptsLead: Each card has the few points interviewers probe and a line you can say out loud. Skip anything not here.
toolsLead: Know what each is for and when you would pick it. Use means do it hands-on in the plan; Know means a one-line explanation is enough.

concepts.t: How LLMs behave, for a PM
concepts.s: Enough to be credible with engineers

l: Models read and write tokens. Cost and latency scale with tokens in and out, and the context window caps what the model sees at once.
Output is probabilistic: the same input can give different answers, so you specify behaviour with examples and tests, not exact rules.
Hallucination is confident wrong output. You reduce it with grounding, constraints and checks; you never remove it entirely.
Quality, cost and latency trade against each other. Bigger models are usually better, slower and pricier.

concepts.say: I think of an LLM feature as a probabilistic component: I specify it with examples, measure it with an eval set, and design the product around its failure modes.

concepts.s: The first question in most AI PM cases

l: Start from the user problem and the cost of a wrong answer, not from the model.
Compare options: a rule or a template, classic ML (prediction, ranking), or an LLM (language, unstructured input, open-ended output).
Good AI fits: tolerant of occasional errors, high volume, value from speed or personalisation, a human can review. Poor fits: zero-error tasks with no review.
Prioritise by impact, feasibility (data, accuracy needed, latency) and risk.

concepts.say: I ask what a wrong answer costs and who catches it. If the cost is low or a human reviews, AI is a candidate; otherwise I start with a simpler solution.

concepts.t: Prompting, structured output and tool use
concepts.s: What you must be able to spec

l: A prompt is part of the product: system instructions, examples and constraints, versioned and tested like code.
Structured output (a JSON schema) lets downstream code rely on the answer. Tool or function calling lets the model request an action your code performs.
As PM you write the behaviour spec: tone, what to refuse, what to cite, how to handle missing information. Engineers turn it into prompts.

concepts.say: I write behaviour specs with good and bad examples, and I expect every prompt change to be tested against the same eval set.

l: Retrieval-augmented generation fetches relevant passages and gives them to the model so answers come from your content, with citations.
Use RAG when knowledge changes often or must be traceable; fine-tuning is for style or format, not for facts.
Failure modes: the right document is never retrieved, stale content, ignoring the retrieved text, and leaking content a user should not see.
Product levers: which sources are in scope, freshness, permissions, and what the product does when nothing relevant is found.

concepts.say: Grounding is a product decision as much as a technical one: which sources, who can see what, and what we say when we do not know.

l: A workflow follows fixed steps with model calls. An agent lets the model choose steps and tools. Prefer a workflow unless the path really varies.
Autonomy is a dial: suggest, draft, act with approval, act alone. Raise it only as measured reliability and reversibility allow.
Risks compound across steps. Add approvals for irreversible actions, spending caps and clear logs of what the agent did.

concepts.say: I start with the lowest autonomy that still delivers value and earn higher autonomy with evidence and reversible actions.

concepts.s: The standard AI PM question: how do you know it works?

l: A golden set of real and tricky cases with expected behaviour, scored by a rubric, by humans, or by an LLM judge that you spot-check against human labels.
Error analysis: read failures, group them, and fix the biggest group first. This guides the roadmap better than a single score.
Task success, edit or accept rate, escalation to a human, thumbs up and down, retention, and guardrail metrics such as complaints or unsafe outputs.
A/B tests work, but sample quality by reading conversations too. Averages hide bad tails.

concepts.say: Nothing ships without a golden set and a pass bar written in the PRD, and every production failure becomes a new test case.

l: Set expectations: say what the feature can and cannot do, and show confidence or sources where it helps.
Make correction cheap: edit, regenerate, undo, and give feedback in one click. Feedback is also your data.
Handle failure on purpose: "I am not sure", a fallback to search or a human, and no dead ends.
Latency is UX: stream partial answers, show progress, and cap long waits.

concepts.say: Trust is earned with sources, easy correction and honest failure states, and I design those before polishing the happy path.

concepts.t: Economics: cost, latency and build vs buy

l: Cost per request is roughly tokens in and out times price, plus retrieval and tooling. Multiply by usage and compare with revenue per user.
Levers: a smaller model for easy cases, caching, shorter prompts, and routing hard cases to a stronger model.
Build vs buy: use a vendor model or API to learn fast; build or fine-tune only for a clear gap in quality, cost, control or data residency.
Pricing options: bundled, usage-based or a premium tier. Watch heavy users who cost more than they pay.

concepts.say: I model unit economics early, route by difficulty to keep cost down, and revisit build vs buy when volume or quality needs change.

concepts.s: Where legal and security get involved

l: Prompt injection: untrusted text can steer the model. Treat model output and tool actions as untrusted and limit permissions.
Privacy: know what data goes to which vendor, retention terms, and how personal data is handled and consented.
Regulation and policy: the EU AI Act and frameworks like the NIST AI RMF classify risk; high-risk uses need documentation and oversight. Confirm current rules with legal.
Red teaming: attack your own feature before launch and log what you fixed.

concepts.say: I involve legal and security at spec time, classify the feature by risk, and treat red-team findings as launch blockers.

concepts.s: What senior and group PM roles probe

l: Moats: proprietary data, distribution, deep workflow integration, and trust. Raw model access is not a moat because competitors can buy it.
Roadmaps under uncertainty: run small experiments, set quality gates, and plan for model upgrades that change what is possible.
Working with engineers, data scientists, designers and legal: shared eval sets, a clear owner for quality, and honest communication about limits.
Launch: staged rollout, guardrail metrics, a feedback loop, and a plan to roll back.

concepts.say: I own the outcome and the quality bar: I define success, make the trade-offs between quality, cost and risk visible, and stage launches so we learn safely.

plan.lead: Weekdays are 3 hours and weekends 5 hours. Weekdays are for reading and short exercises, weekends for the project and mock interviews. One project ties the track together so you can say "I shipped this spec". Select a week to jump to it. Ticks are saved to your account.

project.what: One AI feature for a support or knowledge assistant: problem brief, success metrics, PRD with eval criteria
Working prompt and a grounded answer flow over a small document set, in a chat tool or no-code builder
30-case golden set, a scoring rubric, a run in promptfoo or LangSmith, and an error-analysis table
Failure-state designs, a 10-prompt red-team log, a risk and mitigation list
Cost-per-request sheet, build vs buy note, rollout plan with guardrail metrics

plan.note: Short on time: skip the fine-tuning and MCP notes and one case drill. Keep the project and the mock interviews. Each week is 5 weekdays at 3 h plus a weekend of 10 h, shown as 7 tasks.

weeks.o: Problem brief and a working prompt prototype
tasks: 3|Read concepts 2.1 and 2.2; watch the Karpathy intro video
3|Read concept 2.3; try structured output in a chat tool
3|Pick the project feature (support or knowledge assistant) and list user problems
3|Write the problem brief: user, pain, success metric, cost of a wrong answer
3|Compare rule, classic ML and LLM for the feature in a short table
6|Build the prompt prototype with 10 real example questions
4|Review the prototype failures; note what the PRD must cover

weeks.o: Grounded prototype and an autonomy decision
tasks: 3|Read concept 2.4; read the RAG paper abstract and intro
3|Collect 8 to 10 documents and decide which sources are in scope
3|Read concept 2.5 and the Anthropic agents article
3|Decide the autonomy level for your feature and what needs approval
3|Write what the product does when nothing relevant is found
6|Prototype grounded answers with citations over your documents
4|Test 15 questions; log wrong, missing and ungrounded answers

weeks.o: Golden set, rubric and an error-analysis table
tasks: 3|Read concept 2.6 and the Hamel Husain evals article
3|Write a scoring rubric: correct, grounded, safe, tone
3|Draft 15 golden cases covering normal and tricky inputs
3|Extend to 30 cases including refusals and out-of-scope questions
3|Set up promptfoo or LangSmith and run the set
6|Do error analysis: group failures and rank them by impact
4|Write the pass bar and online metrics for the PRD

weeks.o: Failure-state designs and a red-team log
tasks: 3|Read concept 2.7 and the Google PAIR guidebook sections on trust and errors
3|Sketch the happy path with sources, feedback and correction
3|Design three failure states: unsure, wrong, unavailable
3|Read concept 2.9 and the OWASP LLM Top 10 list
3|List data flows, vendors and personal data in your feature
6|Red-team your prototype with 10 attacks; log fixes
4|Write the risk and mitigation list and name who signs off

weeks.o: Unit-economics sheet and a strategy note
tasks: 3|Read concept 2.8; list cost components for one request
3|Build the cost-per-request sheet with three usage scenarios
3|Write a build vs buy note with a trigger for revisiting it
3|Read concept 2.10; write a one-paragraph moat statement
3|Draft a 3-quarter roadmap with quality gates between steps
6|Price the feature: options, margin, and heavy-user risk
4|Present the economics and strategy aloud in 10 minutes

weeks.o: Finished PRD, rollout plan and mock interviews done
tasks: 3|Write the PRD: problem, users, behaviour spec, eval criteria, failure handling
3|Write the rollout plan: stages, guardrail metrics, rollback
3|Prepare 5 stories on AI trade-offs, a failure, and a launch
3|Drill 3 AI product-sense cases out loud
3|Drill 2 AI strategy and metrics cases out loud
6|Two full mock interviews with a peer; collect feedback
4|Revise answers and re-read the weak concepts
